name: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
title: Checking Claims Against the Ledger
answer: Checking claims against the ledger is the practice of testing sustainability and carbon statements, such as emissions totals, renewable energy use, or credit retirements, against the underlying accounting records that support them. It covers public reports, voluntary disclosures, product claims, and internal management accounts where a figure is asserted and a ledger entry or source document should exist. The work sits between sustainability reporting and financial control, so it draws on emissions inventories, energy invoices, meter readings, procurement records, and general ledger balances. Its purpose is to show whether a claim is traceable, complete, and consistent with the books, not to create a new claim.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Checking claims against the ledger is the practice of testing sustainability and carbon statements, such as emissions totals, renewable energy use, or credit retirements, against the underlying accounting records that support them. It covers public reports, voluntary disclosures, product claims, and internal management accounts where a figure is asserted and a ledger entry or source document should exist. The work sits between sustainability reporting and financial control, so it draws on emissions inventories, energy invoices, meter readings, procurement records, and general ledger balances. Its purpose is to show whether a claim is traceable, complete, and consistent with the books, not to create a new claim.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the systems that already hold the numbers, including ERP and general ledger platforms, carbon accounting software, utility and meter data feeds, emission factor libraries, and document stores for invoices and contracts. Spreadsheets remain common for mapping and reconciliation, while APIs and scheduled exports connect source systems to a review workspace. A ledger of emissions or credits may sit beside the financial ledger, and the two need a shared key such as site, period, entity, or purchase order. Audit trails, version history, and access controls are part of the infrastructure because a check is only as good as the record behind it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts by taking a specific claim and breaking it into the quantities, units, periods, and boundaries that the claim depends on. Those elements are then traced to ledger entries, invoices, meter data, or registry records, and any difference is investigated as a mapping error, a timing issue, a boundary problem, or a genuine gap. Reconciliation and variance analysis are standard, with sampling used where the population is large. AI can help by extracting figures from PDFs, matching descriptions across systems, flagging unusual patterns, and drafting an evidence trail, but a person still reviews the exceptions and the judgment calls. The output is a documented bridge from claim to source, not just a pass or fail.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on evidence, provenance, and the rules that apply to the disclosure. A claim that cannot be tied to a controlled record creates greenwashing risk, assurance risk, and possible regulatory exposure, while weak data lineage makes it hard to defend a number under review. Provenance matters for emission factors, credit registries, and third party data, because the same figure can mean different things depending on its source and vintage. Internal controls, segregation of duties, and clear ownership of the ledger and the claim are the usual safeguards. Regulatory expectations are moving quickly, and the surrounding compliance and regulation landscape is part of the operating context.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more continuous checking, where claims are tested as transactions post rather than once a year. That means tighter links between carbon accounts and financial ledgers, more use of registry data and meter feeds, and more automated evidence collection. Assurance providers and regulators are likely to ask for the same traceability that financial audit already expects, so the boundary between sustainability reporting and internal control will keep thinning. AI will take on more of the matching and extraction work, while the harder questions of boundary, materiality, and intent remain with people. The practical result is that a sustainability claim will increasingly be treated as an accounting assertion with a ledger behind it.
